solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Animal bound to go after some chips

indicators.note: one piece is placed after the other, so the stake comes first and the leap follows it

parts.note: an ante is the stake of chips put in before a poker hand
to lope is to run with long bounding strides

explanation.surface: A creature leaps off to chase a portion of fried potatoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chips' suggests food, but here they are poker chips, and ANTE is the stake put in before the deal.
explanation.definitionFit: The antelope is a swift, horned grazing mammal of Africa and Asia, an example of an animal.

clue.text: Purposeless commercial break

parts.note: an ad is a commercial, an advertisement
a rift is a break or split

explanation.surface: A pointless advertising break on television.
explanation.walkthrough: 'commercial break' reads as one TV phrase but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Being adrift means drifting without direction or aim, so lacking purpose.

clue.text: Fishy character suppressing yen to attempt scam

indicators.note: suppressing means holding down within, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: Triton is the merman sea god of Greek myth, half fish
Y is the abbreviation for the Japanese yen

explanation.surface: A dodgy individual sits on a yen as part of a swindle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fishy' suggests dishonest, but Triton is literally half fish.
explanation.definitionFit: To try it on is a British idiom for attempting to deceive or take advantage of someone.

clue.text: Female rider that jockeys avidly goad

indicators.note: jockeys as a verb means manoeuvres or shifts about, so the letters are moved around

explanation.surface: A horsewoman whom racing jockeys eagerly spur on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jockeys' reads as riders, but is a verb that jostles the letters of AVIDLY GOAD.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady Godiva is the legendary noblewoman who rode naked through Coventry, a famous horsewoman.

clue.text: Current fashion?

parts.note: current reads as present-day, but it is electric current, so power, and fashion is a style of dress

explanation.surface: What is trendy right now in clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' means electrical power here, and fashion is dressing.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names an assertive 1980s business style of clothing meant to convey authority.

clue.text: This person talks a long time: flipping endlessly

indicators.note: flipping turns the combined letters over, so the run is read backwards

parts.note: to gab is to chatter, so talks gives gabs

indicators.note: endlessly says the final letter of the word for a long time is dropped

parts.note: an age is a long time

explanation.surface: Someone says of themselves that they chatter on and on, cursing endlessly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' looks like a mild British expletive but is the reversal signal, applied to the whole run GABSAG; 'endlessly' trims AGE. The clue as a whole describes the person.
explanation.definitionFit: The person the clue describes, one who talks a long time, is a windbag or chatterbox.

clue.text: Answer recognised when heard again

indicators.note: when heard says the word is spoken and the spelling follows its sound

parts.note: knew means recognised, past tense of know

explanation.surface: An answer was identified when it was listened to again.
explanation.walkthrough: KNEW, 'recognised', sounds like NEW.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something anew means doing it afresh or once more.

clue.text: Caterpillar turning an age to undergo rapid development

indicators.note: turning means turned round, so the larva word is read backwards

parts.note: a grub is an insect larva such as a caterpillar
an eon is an age, a vast span of time

explanation.surface: A caterpillar changes over time and grows fast into a butterfly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' reverses GRUB into BURG; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To burgeon is to grow or flourish quickly, like buds bursting.

clue.text: Poorly made glove has split down the middle

indicators.note: poorly made means badly put together, so the letters are reassembled differently

explanation.surface: A shoddily made glove has torn along its centre seam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poorly made' rearranges GLOVE HAS.
explanation.definitionFit: To go halves is to share costs equally, dividing them fifty-fifty.

clue.text: Beam that's almost three feet round

indicators.note: round says the shortened word is turned about and read backwards
almost says the last letter of the measure is missing

parts.note: a yard is three feet

explanation.surface: A shaft of light measuring nearly a yard across.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims YARD to YAR, and 'round' reverses those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A ray is a narrow beam of light or other radiation.

clue.text: Grounded because of dodgy heart

parts.note: something down to a cause is due to it, so because of gives down to

indicators.note: dodgy means unsound or unreliable, so the letters of the following word are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is grounded from flying owing to an unreliable heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dodgy' rearranges HEART into EARTH.
explanation.definitionFit: A grounded person is sensible and practical, the idiomatic meaning of the hyphenated phrase.

clue.text: Pseudoscientific movement to interpolate blunders

indicators.note: blunders, as a verb, means stumbles about clumsily, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A fringe science movement makes errors when inserting material.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blunders' reads as a noun but is a verb acting on TO INTERPOLATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Instant transport of matter across space is a staple of science fiction with no basis in real science.

clue.text: Appropriate opening of zoo with Mr Durrell, a writer

parts.note: fit means suitable or appropriate

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter

parts.note: Gerald Durrell was the naturalist who founded Jersey Zoo

explanation.surface: A writer comes along with zoo founder Gerald Durrell to open the zoo.
explanation.walkthrough: Gerald Durrell, the naturalist and writer, founded Jersey Zoo, which fits the zoo surface.
explanation.definitionFit: F. Scott Fitzgerald, author of The Great Gatsby, is a famous American novelist.

clue.text: You will quaintly call out

parts.note: ye is the archaic form of you, which 'quaintly' points to
'll is the shortened form of will, written in the old-fashioned way after ye

explanation.surface: An archaic way of saying you will shout.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as the contraction YE'LL, the apostrophe dropped, the letters spell the shout.
explanation.definitionFit: To yell is to shout or cry out loudly.

clue.text: Police assistant has possible cold case to pursue

parts.note: a case of the cold, someone who sniffs, is a sniffer
to dog is to follow or pursue relentlessly

explanation.surface: A detective's helper takes on an unsolved old case to investigate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cold case' suggests an unsolved crime, but means a person with a cold.
explanation.definitionFit: Police use trained dogs to detect drugs or explosives by scent, a canine helper.

clue.text: Comparatively mean returns in restructured insurance

indicators.note: returns says the hidden letters are read backwards
in says the letters lie inside the run of words that follows

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A shrewder, stingier insurance policy comes back after restructuring.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft left 'in' unparsed; it is the hidden-word signal, and 'returns' reverses the letters found in 'restructuRED INSurance'.
explanation.definitionFit: Snide means sneering or spiteful, so the comparative form is more mean in spirit.

clue.text: Coppers accepting an act of contrition

indicators.note: accepting means taking in, so one word holds the other inside it

parts.note: coppers are low-value copper coins, pennies, so pence

explanation.surface: Police officers take on an act of contrition, perhaps repenting a bribe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coppers' suggests police, but here it means copper coins: PENCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Penance is a self-punishment or devotion undertaken to show sorrow for wrongdoing.

clue.text: At least a dozen deliveries, stolen or missed

parts.note: in cricket an over is six balls, so two or more overs is at least twelve deliveries
hot is slang for stolen goods

explanation.surface: Several overs of bowling, either pinched or failing to hit.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is six deliveries bowled by one bowler, so plural overs make twelve or more.
explanation.definitionFit: Overshot means went past the target, so missed it.

clue.text: Partial duplication of travel document is concerning

indicators.note: partial says the doubled run is not complete, losing its final letter
duplication means the word appears twice in a row

parts.note: a visa is an entry permit stamped in a passport

explanation.surface: A partially copied visa raises questions about something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'duplication of' gives VISAVISA; 'Partial' drops the last A.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase means face to face, and in English it is used as a preposition meaning regarding or in relation to.

clue.text: Winter figure, small currently, lots having been cut

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as in clothing sizes
now means at present, currently

indicators.note: having been cut says the final letter of the word is lopped off

parts.note: many means lots

explanation.surface: A wintry character, small at present, after many were cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having been cut' trims MANY to MAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A figure built of packed snow is the classic winter outdoor creation.

clue.text: Unusual urge to put iron back inside safe place

indicators.note: to put means to place, here signalling that one piece is placed within another
the reversed metal symbol goes within the rearranged letters
unusual means out of the ordinary, so the letters are rearranged
back says the chemical symbol is reversed

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

explanation.surface: A strange impulse to carry the iron back into a shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusual' gives RUGE from the letters of 'urge', and 'to put ... inside' places the reversed symbol after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A refuge is a shelter or sanctuary offering protection from danger.

clue.text: Have problems navigating on your bike!

definitions.meaning: to lose your way, failing to find the route
British slang for go away, clear off

explanation.surface: Struggling to find the way while cycling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On your bike!' is a British dismissal meaning go away.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses of the phrase fit: losing your way, and the rude command to leave.

clue.text: Bird like this turned up by quarry

indicators.note: in a down clue turned up means read from bottom to top, so reversed

parts.note: so means in this way, like this
quarry is hunted prey

explanation.surface: A bird such as this one appeared near a stone pit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quarry' suggests a stone pit, but means hunted prey.
explanation.definitionFit: The osprey is a fish-eating bird of prey, also called the sea hawk.

clue.text: Informal jumper: knitter's first piece

parts.note: roo is the informal Australian word for kangaroo, a famous jumper

indicators.note: first takes just the first letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A casual sweater that is the first thing a knitter makes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jumper' suggests a British sweater, but it is a kangaroo, ROO informally. The definition 'piece' is a chess piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The rook, or castle, is one of the pieces in chess.

clue.text: Charlie and I get a rest arranged — we're puffed!

parts.note: Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: arranged means put into a new order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Two exhausted friends arrange a break because they are out of breath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'puffed' reads as British slang for breathless, but the definition means smoked: cigarettes are puffed on.
explanation.definitionFit: Smokers draw on cigarettes in puffs, so they are the things being puffed.

clue.text: European city is area under pressure

indicators.note: in a down clue the later pieces sit below the first, so they come after it

parts.note: P is the physics symbol for pressure

explanation.surface: A European city whose area is under strain.
explanation.walkthrough: Being a down clue, 'is area under pressure' places IS A beneath P.
explanation.definitionFit: Pisa is the Italian city in Tuscany famous for its leaning tower.

clue.text: High flyer?

parts.note: a high flyer is an ambitious achiever; here it is a bird that hovers, and humming is slang for smelly, as high is

explanation.surface: An ambitious person, or something that flies far up.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang both 'high' and 'humming' mean smelly, so this flyer is a 'high' bird.
explanation.definitionFit: This tiny hovering bird has a name whose first part is a slang word for stinking, as high is.

clue.text: Board amidships with this?

indicators.note: amidships means in the middle of a ship, so the central letters of the word are taken

explanation.surface: Climbing into a rowing boat in its middle, carrying a paddle.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle of BOARD, without its outside letters, is OAR, and 'this' is what you row with once aboard.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue points at a rowing implement, the long-bladed pole a rower handles in the middle of a boat.

clue.text: Dye covering half of hair in helmet

indicators.note: covering means wrapping round, so the colouring word goes round the other letters

parts.note: a tint is a dye or colouring, especially for hair

indicators.note: half of takes the first two of the four letters

explanation.surface: Hair colour applied to half the head under a helmet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half of' takes the front half of 'hair'; 'covering' wraps the dye word round it.
explanation.definitionFit: A tin hat is a soldier's steel helmet, an informal British name.

clue.text: Noble, like the News at Ten broadcast?

indicators.note: broadcast means spoken out on air, so the word is heard rather than read

parts.note: News at Ten is a British evening news programme shown every night

explanation.surface: A dignified quality, like the evening television news.
explanation.walkthrough: News at Ten is a long-running British TV news bulletin aired each evening.
explanation.definitionFit: Knightly means chivalrous and honourable, befitting a knight, so noble in character.
